newsitem.title: FINLAND: New Amer bid unlikely to fly - analysts.
newsitem.headline: New Amer bid unlikely to fly - analysts.

text.p: Finnish investment company Norvestia's challenge to British investor Lord Moyne's recent bid for control of Finnish sporting goods group Amer-Yhtyma looks unlikely to succeed, analysts said on Friday.
Amer's controlling owners said earlier they are bound by an agreement with Jonathan Bryan Guinness, third Lord Moyne, to refrain from talking to any other bidder for their vote-heavy K-shares.
"I don't think the deal can be reversed just like that," said analyst Jukka Fransas of FSB Securities.
The K shareholders' deal with Guinness presumably involved penalty clauses to keep the sellers from backing out, he said.

Fransas said that although Norvestia could be a better owner for Amer than Lord Moyne because it would, in his view, be more likely to contribute to developing the group, Norvestia was just plain late. "It has been known for two years already that Amer has been for sale," he said.

The uncertainty caused by the competing bids from a little-known British investor and now a last-minute Finnish ownership scheme was not good for Amer's long-term business relationships abroad, Fransas said.
Four Finnish associations, which hold 90.5 percent of Amer's votes mainly through their K-series shares, agreed on June 2 to sell 1.1 million K shares to Guinness for 301 million markka.
This was challenged on Thursday by Norvestia, which said it was interested in becoming a main owner by possibly bidding for some of the K shares at mainly the same terms as Guinness.
"We want to offer an alternative so that the company, if it wants, can still get another kind of owner in the final stretch," Norvestia chief executive Timo Loyttyniemi told Reuters on Friday.

Norvestia's proposal assumes that the K-shareholders will sell their stock, and that Amer's supervisory board can decide to exercise the company's right to redeem the shares at the same price offered by Lord Moyne, he said.
In that case, Norvestia has said it was ready to become the main owner together with one of the present K shareholders.
"My opinion is that this (Norvestia plan) does not have much of a foundation," said Postipankki analyst Teemu Lahkela.
And the K shareholders said they would block such a move.

"We intend to act (on the supervisory board) so that no redemption will happen," Leea Murtolehto, chairman of the Finnish Association of Graduates in Economics and Business Administration (SEFE), told Reuters by telephone.
"According to our agreement (with Guinness), we will not negotiate with anyone else," she said.
"We are all agreed on this," said Tarja Ollilainen-Ahola of the business school's student union, representing a 25 percent stake and referring to all the K-share owners.
"We have committed ourselves to not negotiating," she said.
And Heikki Kauppi, secretary general of the engineers' association which owns 34 percent of K shares, said Norvestia could not do anything to sweeten the offer.
"Even if incomprehensible amounts of money had been offered, we would not be in a position to consider it," he said.

The Finnish Association of Graduate Engineers, the Student Union of the Helsinki School of Economics and Business Administration, SEFE and The Land and Water Technology Foundation -- together own 1.99 million K shares.
The four also own 748,835 listed A shares, giving them 11.5 percent of Amer's capital.
In all, the listed A shares represent 92 percent of capital, and they have preferential dividend rights, but it is the K shares that give voting control.
Some analysts, speaking anonymously, raised doubts about whether the Norvestia move was simply a publicity stunt, but Loyttyniemi assured Reuters that his company is serious about the plan.
"We are a long-term investor, so we would bring the kind of ownership that the company has long been looking for," Loyttyniemi said.
